passages.t: A body in the field, and no one to blame
passages.happening:
A person is found killed in open country, ‘and it is not known who killed him’ (verse 1). The elders and judges are to measure which town is nearest (verse 2).

The elders of that town take a young cow that has never worked, bring it to a valley with a running stream, and break its neck there (verses 3-4). The priests come forward. Then the elders wash their hands over the animal and say, “Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it. Accept this atonement, O LORD, for Your people Israel whom You have redeemed, and do not hold the shedding of innocent blood against them” (verses 7-8).

‘And the bloodshed will be atoned for’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Every ancient society had to decide who was answerable when a body was found and no killer could be named. The law of Hammurabi of Babylon made the city and its governor pay the victim's family. Deuteronomy also makes the nearest town answerable. But here the town answers to God.

What the law will not do is shrug. A person has been killed, and no one has been charged. In this book the shedding of innocent blood stains the land, and it cannot simply be left. An unknown victim in a field still matters to God, and so must matter to the nearest town.

The rite is strange to a modern reader. It should be seen for what it does. The leaders of the town must come out in public. They must stand over the death, say that they neither did it nor saw it, and pray. The washing of hands is a sign of innocence. The prayer does more than deny. It asks God to ‘accept this atonement’ for his people. The elders do not treat themselves as beyond question. They ask for mercy for the whole community.

The Hebrew word for ‘atonement’ is used across the Old Testament for the covering or wiping away of guilt, so that the bond with God is made whole.

The law teaches that a community has a duty toward a death it did not cause and cannot solve. No one may say that it is not their concern.
passages.later:
The first murder in the Bible was also in a field, and God said of it, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10).

Numbers gives the principle behind the rite: ‘bloodshed pollutes the land’ (Numbers 35:33).

The Roman governor Pilate used the same sign when he sent Jesus to die: “he took water and washed his hands before the crowd. ‘I am innocent of this man’s blood,’ he said” (Matthew 27:24). The elders of this law could say it truthfully. Pilate could not.
passages.asks: The town nearest the body had to come out and answer for it, though no one there had done it. Ask what suffering close to you is no one's fault in particular and so has become no one's concern. And ask whether your community prays over the harm done in its midst, or only says that it was not to blame.

passages.happening:
The law turns to a case from war. Israel has defeated an enemy and taken captives. A soldier sees ‘a beautiful woman among them’ and wants her as his wife (verses 10-11).

He must bring her into his house. She is to shave her head, trim her nails and put off the clothes she was captured in (verses 12-13). She is to live in his house ‘a full month’ and mourn her father and mother. Only then may he take her as his wife.

“And if you are not pleased with her, you are to let her go wherever she wishes. But you must not sell her for money or treat her as a slave, since you have dishonored her” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the most painful laws in the book, and it has to be read honestly. It is about a woman whose people have been defeated in war. She has been taken by the army that defeated them. She is not asked whether she wishes to marry.

That is in the text, and it cannot be explained away. These notes do not defend it.

It helps to see the world the law was speaking into. In ancient war, women who were captured were commonly raped or sold as slaves.

Into that world this law puts limits on the soldier. He must take her into his household. He must wait a full month. During that month she is allowed to grieve. The shaved head, the trimmed nails and the change of clothes marked the end of her old life, and the month gave her time to mourn her father and mother. If he marries her, she is a wife and not a slave. If he later sends her away, she goes free. He may not sell her.

The last words of the law are the law's own judgment on what has happened: ‘you have dishonored her’. The law does not call this good. It names the wrong done to her, and it gives that wrong as the reason she must not be treated as property.

So the law does two things, and a reader must hold both. It restrained a common cruelty. And it still allowed a man to take a woman who had no choice. The hard question below goes further.
passages.later:
The first chapter of the Bible says of every human being what this law's world forgot: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27).

The law of Moses punished the seizing of a person with death: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16).

Jesus said of another law in this book, the law of divorce, “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart; but it was not this way from the beginning” (Matthew 19:8).
passages.hard:
How can God's law allow a soldier to take a captive woman as a wife?

A reader is right to be troubled, and no answer should try to make the trouble go away.

The law permits a great deal. A woman captured in war could be taken as a wife by one of the men who captured her. Her consent is not asked. That is in the text.

The law also sets limits. He must wait a month. He must let her mourn. He must marry her and not merely use her. If he rejects her she goes free, and she can never be sold or made a slave. In a world where captured women were raped or sold as a matter of course, these were real restraints.

Many interpreters read this law as Jesus read the law of divorce: a rule given because of the hardness of human hearts. On this reading it does not show what God wants. It limits harm in a violent world and moves that world toward justice. Others stress that in its setting the law gave real protection to a woman with no protector. Critics answer that it still allowed a forced marriage, and that this must be faced. Each of these is true to the text.

Some things must be said plainly. This law is not a pattern for today. It gives no army and no man any right over any woman. Rape, forced marriage and the abuse of captives are grave evils. They are crimes, and nothing in the Bible excuses them.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law would not let a soldier forget that his captive was a daughter with a father and mother to mourn. Ask whom you are tempted to treat as something to be used and not as a person with a history and a grief. And if this passage has opened an old wound, do not carry it alone.

passages.t: The son of the wife who is not loved
passages.happening:
A man has two wives, ‘one beloved and the other unloved’. Both have sons, and the firstborn is the son of the wife he does not love (verse 15).

When he divides his property, he may not give the place of the firstborn to the son of the wife he prefers (verse 16). “Instead, he must acknowledge the firstborn, the son of his unloved wife, by giving him a double portion of all that he has” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Inheritance in Israel passed mainly to sons, and the firstborn received a double share. With it came the duty of leading the family after the father's death.

The law takes for granted that a man might have more than one wife. That was allowed in Israel. It was never commanded, and the Bible's own stories show the misery it caused. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and the favor he showed one wife became favor for her sons and hatred among the brothers.

This law says that a father's feelings do not decide a child's rights. He may love one wife more than the other. He may not make her son pay for it. The child of the unloved woman keeps what is his.

It is a law for the protection of the weaker party in a household: a wife out of favor, and a son with no one to plead for him against his own father.
passages.later:
Genesis tells the story behind the law: Jacob ‘loved Rachel more than Leah’, and “When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb” (Genesis 29:30-31). God took the side of the wife who was not loved.

Jacob used the words of verse 17 of his own firstborn, Leah's son: “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength” (Genesis 49:3).
passages.asks: The law would not let a father's preference cost a child what was due to him. Ask whether your likes and dislikes decide how fairly you treat people who depend on you: children, employees or members of a church. And remember whom God noticed in Jacob's house.

passages.happening:
A man has ‘a stubborn and rebellious son’ who will not obey his father and mother or listen when they correct him (verse 18).

His father and mother are to bring him to the elders at the gate of the town and say, ‘This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey us. He is a glutton and a drunkard’ (verses 19-20).

“Then all the men of his city will stone him to death. So you must purge the evil from among you, and all Israel will hear and be afraid” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
This law shocks a modern reader, and it should be read slowly.

The son in view is not a small child, and he is not a child who has misbehaved once. He is described as ‘a glutton and a drunkard’, which is not a description of a small child. The Hebrew word for ‘rebellious’ means settled defiance and not a single act. He has been corrected and has refused.

In many ancient societies a father had the power of life and death over his children. This law takes that power out of the father's hands. He cannot act by himself. The mother must agree and must speak. The case must go to the elders of the town, in public, at the gate. A father's anger is not enough.

So the law that sounds like a threat to children was, in its world, a limit on fathers.

Jewish interpreters hedged the law with so many conditions that it could hardly be applied. A view recorded in the Talmud holds that there never was a case of the stubborn and rebellious son.

The hard question below says what this law does not permit.
passages.later:
Jesus was called by the words of this law. His enemies said of him, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’ (Matthew 11:19). The New Testament does not itself connect the two passages.

Jesus told a story about a son who took his share of the family's wealth and ‘squandered his wealth in wild living’ (Luke 15:13). When that son came home, the father did not take him to the gate. “He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).
passages.hard:
Does this law give parents a right to harm a child who will not obey?

No. It never did, and it does not now.

In its own setting the law took the power over a child's life away from the father and put the matter before the whole town, with the mother's voice required. Jewish tradition narrowed it until, on one view, it was never carried out. Many Christian interpreters read it, with other laws in this chapter, as a rule given for a hard world, aimed at restraint, and not as a picture of what God desires.

It is a law of ancient Israel. It is not given to the church or to any family. No one may use it to justify striking, threatening or harming a child, or driving a son or daughter out of the home.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law put a father's anger under the judgment of others. Ask who checks your anger at home, and whether you would be willing to have your treatment of your children seen by the whole town. And set the father in Jesus' story beside this law. Ask which of the two your own children would say they have met.

passages.happening:
The last law is about the body of a man who has been put to death for a crime. If his body is hung on a tree, “you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day, because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse” (verse 23).

The reason is added: “You must not defile the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance.”
passages.hearers:
The hanging here was not the way the man was killed. He was already dead. In the ancient world the body of an executed person was sometimes put up on a tree or a post as a public warning.

The law limits even that. The body must come down the same day and be buried. However great the crime, the dead man is not to be left exposed through the night. He is still a human being, and the land must not be made unclean by his unburied body.

To be hung up like this was the deepest public disgrace. The law says that such a person is ‘under God’s curse’: he stands under God's judgment in the sight of all.

Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, one text discusses this law in connection with hanging a living person. Many scholars take that to mean crucifixion, the Roman way of execution. By the first century a man who died on a cross looked, to anyone who knew this verse, like a man God had rejected.
passages.later:
Joshua kept this law with the body of a defeated king: ‘at sunset Joshua commanded that they take down the body from the tree’ (Joshua 8:29).

The same law lies behind what happened on the day Jesus died. The bodies were not to be left hanging overnight, and so the request was made that they be taken down (John 19:31). Jesus was buried before sunset.

The apostles spoke of his death in the words of this verse. Peter said, ‘whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree’ (Acts 5:30). The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains why words like these are a call from a Jew to his own people and never a charge against the Jewish people.

Paul quotes the verse to say what the cross means. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13). A crucified Messiah seemed impossible, because a man hung on a tree was under God's curse. Paul does not deny it. He says that Jesus did bear the curse, and bore it for others, ‘in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles’ (Galatians 3:14).

That is the New Testament's own reading of this verse.
passages.asks: The law gave even an executed criminal a burial before dark. Ask whether there is anyone you think is beyond the reach of ordinary human respect. And consider what Paul says: that Christ took the place of the one under the curse. Ask what it means for you that he was willing to be counted there.
